ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A vertical cylindrical tube of mass $M$ is positioned such that its lower end is at a height $H$ above the horizontal ground. A small ball of mass $m$ is placed at the top of the tube. The tube is released from rest and falls freely, undergoing multiple elastic collisions with the ground, with each collision occurring over an infinitesimally short time. The tube maintains a vertical orientation throughout the motion. Given that $M=4m$, the magnitude of the sliding frictional force between the ball and the tube is $4mg$, where $g$ is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration. Air resistance is neglected.

1. Determine the magnitudes of the accelerations of the tube and the ball immediately after the first collision of the tube with the ground.
2. After the tube bounces for the first time, assuming the ball does not slide out of the tube during its upward motion, calculate the maximum height the tube reaches.
3. During the upward motion after the second bounce, the ball still does not slide out of the tube. Determine the condition that the length of the circular tube must satisfy.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: The attached diagrams show a vertical tube represented by two black vertical sides, with a small ball located at the top opening of the tube. A blue dashed vertical line indicates the vertical fall direction through the tube and down to a hatched horizontal ground. A blue dashed horizontal line marks the level of the lower end of the tube, and a double arrow labeled H shows that this lower end is initially height H above the ground. Use upward as positive. Just before the first collision with the ground, the tube and ball have both fallen through height H, so their speed is v = sqrt(2gH) downward. The ground collision is elastic and instantaneous, so only the tube velocity reverses: immediately after the collision, the tube has velocity +v, while the ball still has velocity -v. Because the tube moves upward relative to the ball, the ball slides downward relative to the tube. Thus kinetic friction on the ball is upward with magnitude 4mg, and friction on the tube is downward with magnitude 4mg. For the tube, M = 4m, so the downward forces are Mg + 4mg = 4mg + 4mg = 8mg. Hence a_T = -(8mg)/(4m) = -2g, so its acceleration magnitude is 2g. For the ball, upward friction is 4mg and downward weight is mg, so the net force is 3mg upward. Hence a_b = +3g, so its acceleration magnitude is 3g. For the first rebound height, during the sliding phase the relative velocity is initially v_b - v_T = -v - v = -2v, and the relative acceleration is a_b - a_T = 3g - (-2g) = 5g. Sliding stops when the relative velocity becomes zero: -2v + 5gt = 0, so t = 2v/(5g). In this time the tube displacement is s_T = vt + (1/2)(-2g)t^2 = vt - gt^2. Substituting t = 2v/(5g) and v^2 = 2gH gives s_T = 12H/25. At that instant, the common velocity is v_T = v - 2gt = v - 4v/5 = v/5. Then the tube and ball move together freely upward under gravity, adding height (v/5)^2/(2g) = H/25. Therefore the maximum height after the first bounce is H_1 = 12H/25 + H/25 = 13H/25. For the tube length condition, compute downward relative slip of the ball in the tube. During the first upward sliding phase, the relative displacement is |(-2v)t + (1/2)(5g)t^2| = 2v^2/(5g) = 4H/5. After the first maximum height, the tube falls again from height H_1, so just before the second collision its speed satisfies u^2 = 2gH_1. After the second elastic bounce, the same relative-motion calculation gives additional downward slip 2u^2/(5g) = 4H_1/5 = 4(13H/25)/5 = 52H/125. For the ball not to slide out during the upward motion after the second bounce, the tube length must be at least the cumulative slip: L >= 4H/5 + 52H/125 = 152H/125.
